essay_bank.personal_statement: Growing up near the Charles River, I watched a decade of restoration work turn a polluted waterway into a place where herons nest again. That project taught me environmental science is never just biology or chemistry in isolation — it is biology and chemistry braided together with policy, funding, and the patience to work with a community for years rather than weeks. I spent the last two summers volunteering with a coastal wetlands monitoring program, logging water quality data that eventually fed into a state permitting decision. Seeing our measurements cited in an actual regulatory document was the moment I stopped thinking of environmental science as a subject I was good at and started thinking of it as a career I wanted. I am pursuing a degree in environmental science with a focus on climate policy because I want to be one of the people translating field data into decisions that hold up in a hearing room, not just a lab report. This scholarship would let me spend next summer on a full-time research fellowship instead of a part-time job, which is the difference between doing the work I care about and just reading about people who get to.
